title: Rome Cracks Down on Tourist Golf Carts
paragraphs: In recent years, electric golf carts carrying tourists have become an increasingly familiar sight in the narrow streets of Rome's historic center. However, city authorities, responding to complaints from residents, are now moving to bring the booming business under control.

According to reports in September 2026, there are now as many as 500 golf carts operating in Rome. Their popularity has soared, with bookings this summer rising by 147% compared with 2024, according to the travel company TripAdvisor, whose subsidiary Viator is the largest source of passengers. For tourists, the attraction is obvious: in a matter of hours, a cart can take them past many of the city's major sights without the need for long walks.

Nevertheless, critics argue that the carts are adding to congestion in an area that is already heavily crowded. The historic center has only around 4,300 regular on-street parking spaces, roughly a quarter of the number of cars owned by its residents, and approximately 50,000 vehicles enter it every day. Residents have also complained about carts parking illegally. Luigi la Licata, the head of a local neighborhood association, described the golf cart as the latest and most obvious of many types of vehicles that have added to the traffic.

In response, Rome's deputy mayor for mobility, Eugenio Patanè, wants to establish fixed routes for tours, limit the total number of carts and introduce a system for selecting operators. However, the city must first receive the necessary regulatory powers from the regional government. According to Patanè, cities facing this phenomenon currently have "very few weapons."

Operators, on the other hand, warn that the proposed rules could severely damage their young industry. Pascal van Duijnhoven, the president of an association of tour operators, acknowledged that overtourism is a real problem but argued that carts could be part of the solution, since they are quiet, produce no exhaust and take up less space than tourist buses. Supporters also point out that carts make the city more accessible for visitors with limited mobility.
Meanwhile, the city of Florence has gone further, banning tourist golf carts and rickshaws from its historic center.
